note: Contrarian pass, steel-man-the-premise angle: the plan's structure is strong, so I pressed on its load-bearing premises — the sequencing rationale, the writer-model's ordering guarantees, the parity-gate semantics, and the unexamined interactions with existing safety machinery.

findings.topic: supervisor split vs zombie-hunter live-owner semantics
findings.message: The plan moves job ownership into a separate process but never mentions the armed orphan-kill machinery that keys off in-process job state. Today's orphan discriminator (zombie_hunter.live_owner_ids) computes 'live owner' from the DASHBOARD'S view: PTY-attached set ∪ job_runner._holder_is_active ∪ parent-owned. Post-split, the dashboard no longer holds the job handles — _holder_is_active in the dashboard process will report supervisor-owned jobs as NOT active, so a supervisor-owned session with no open browser stream becomes classifiable as an orphan and the Swarm View / armed kill-daemon can freeze or kill exactly the work the split exists to protect. The repo marks this discriminator SAFETY-CRITICAL (2026-06-30). The in-memory rebuild table covers dashboard structures (_LIVE, _JOB_DIRS, lane locks) but zombie-hunter's live-owner provider is not a rebuild row and is not named anywhere in Phase 5. The C4 live demo could pass (short window, daemon not firing) while the regression ships. Phase 5 needs an explicit row: live_owner_ids' job_active provider must query the supervisor (or the merged journal) before the external seam goes live.

findings.section: Dependency DAG & sequencing rationale / Phase 4 exit gate
findings.message: The DAG edge 'Phase 5 after Phase 4' is justified by IPC reusing the route-table module + token helper — but that module exists on DAY ONE of Phase 4 (rows-first: every route gets a declared row immediately). What the plan actually gates Phase 5 behind is Phase 4's new C2-BLOCKING exit gate: migrating ~125 handler bodies to zero legacy arms across 3–4 waves. The supervisor consumes none of that handler migration. Meanwhile C4 — the restart-survival keystone the North Star calls non-negotiable, and the one pillar relieving John's real daily pain (every restart kills in-flight jobs) — lands last among pillars, behind weeks of mechanical body migration, and every per-wave smoke ritual in Phases 0–4 performs an nssm restart that kills any in-flight job. Steel-manning the plan's own 'highest-value first' re-cut logic (used to pull the journal forward), the same logic says Phase 5's jobs-half can start once the table module + warn-mode auth + the Phase-3 ownership table exist, concurrent with or immediately after the enforce flips — not after the zero-arms drive-down. The hard gate is right for C2; making it a prerequisite for C4 is an over-constrained edge the DAG should either relax or explicitly defend.

findings.section: Phase 3 — journal-first write order / two-tier parity gate
findings.message: Two commitments contradict. Journal-first-by-decree says an orphaned journal event (emit succeeded, legacy write then failed or the process crashed between them) is 'a benign intent record with an idempotent replay path.' The Tier-2 gate says journal-ahead OLDER than the tail window 'is classified BUG.' The crash-between-writes case — the exact scenario journal-first is designed to make benign — produces precisely a beyond-window journal-ahead event, so the designed-for, called-benign failure mode is permanently flagged BUG by the gate that proves C3. Either the classification needs a reconciled/acknowledged state (journal-ahead + replay-tool-converged → resolved, not BUG), or 'benign' is the wrong word and the plan should say every orphan is a defect requiring operator replay. As written, the first real crash makes the daily parity gate red forever with no defined path back to green, which corrodes the gate's authority (C7's 'suite stays green' meets a gate that can't self-heal).

findings.topic: wall-clock merge order not causally safe
findings.section: The journal writer model — seq/lock semantics
findings.message: The total order for derivation, parity, and replay is sort-by (ts, writer_id, writer_seq). Wall clocks — even on one machine — step backwards (NTP correction, resume-from-sleep on a desktop that sleeps nightly), and ts resolution ties across writers are resolved LEXICALLY, which happens to sort 'dashboard' before 'supervisor' today but is a coincidence, not a design. A causally-ordered pair (dashboard job_launch_requested → supervisor job_launched → supervisor job_finished) can merge out of order under a clock step, and rebuild_index / the replay tool — whose correctness IS criterion C3's 'provably derivable' — silently apply last-write-wins reductions in the wrong order. The envelope already carries causation_id; the merge should use it (or a hybrid logical clock: max(seen_ts+1, wall)) as a tie-and-regression breaker, and the parity gate should classify a causation edge that sorts backwards as BUG. Right now clock regression is the one failure mode NOT in the enumerated six, and it's the one that corrupts derivation rather than just losing a line.

The shim's protection premise has a hole at both ends. (1) Clients that predate the shim deploy — the already-open stale tab and the PWA-cached iPad client, the two named beneficiaries — never send X-Anchor-Build at all, and the plan doesn't say what the server does with a MISSING header. Reject it and you break anchor_healthcheck.py's endpoint walk, the CLI, and every personal script (a C7 breakage in the 'one behavior-bearing deploy'); allow it and every pre-shim client silently bypasses the shim, so the mechanism only protects tabs opened AFTER the deploy that needed protecting least. (2) The carrier rides _postJson only — WS/SSE attach and GET navigations from a stale client carry no build id, so a stale tab can hold a live terminal WebSocket across a protocol-changing deploy unchecked. The shim needs a stated missing-header policy (allow + log, with the banner delivered by a different channel for pre-shim clients, e.g. a version probe on next poll) and an honest statement of which surfaces it does NOT cover.

findings.section: Dependency DAG — Phase 2 before Phase 3 edge
findings.message: The edge is declared 'hard: journals must be born outside the repo, never migrated.' But the journal writes under ANCHOR_DATA_DIR via the existing paths.py seam — if it shipped before the move it would simply relocate with everything else through the same migrate_data pass Phase 2 already runs (append-only JSONL is the EASIEST store to migrate: no absolute paths inside, no rewrite map entries). The real cost of early birth is a week of journal files in git-status noise, solvable with one .gitignore line. Calling a preference a hard dependency matters because it's the stated reason C3 — 'the highest-value pillar' by the plan's own words — can't move earlier than fourth position. Either defend the edge with a real invariant (e.g. the parity gate's fixture paths) or downgrade it to 'preferred ordering' so a future re-cut isn't blocked by a phantom constraint.

findings.topic: per-wave smoke restarts kill in-flight jobs pre-split
findings.message: The drain script parks PTY sessions (close_session + capture_session_docs) but says nothing about in-flight LANE JOBS, which until Phase 5 are children of the dashboard process and die with every nssm restart. The ritual runs at every wave across Phases 0–4 — on the order of 15+ restarts of the live service before restart survival exists. 'Never-broken increments' as John experiences it includes not silently killing a running Foreman build because a wave merged. The ritual needs one more line: check for active jobs (the lane locks / job dirs) and either wait for quiescence or get explicit go-ahead before restarting — otherwise the smoke ritual institutionalizes exactly the loss C4 exists to end.

The live gate derives views from 'a WRITE_LOCK-bracketed snapshot copy' — but WRITE_LOCK is the dashboard's in-process lock. Post-split, the supervisor appends to its segment and mutates job dirs outside that lock, so the snapshot is not consistent across processes: the gate can catch the supervisor between its emit and its legacy job-record write (tolerated as young journal-ahead) but ALSO between a job-dir write and the snapshot of the segment directory listing, producing spurious 'conflict' classifications that are ALWAYS BUG by decree. The plan built the writer model multi-process from day one but left the parity gate's quiescence mechanism single-process. State the cross-process snapshot rule (e.g. read segments AFTER legacy stores, so any skew presents as tolerated journal-ahead, never conflict) or the Phase-5 flip will manufacture flaky reds in the gate that must run 20-consecutive-green.

findings.section: The journal writer model — cli segment locking
findings.message: The cli segment's per-append lock is specified as msvcrt.locking — a Windows-only stdlib module. The inherited constraint (CLAUDE.md, enforced by distro.py's import scan) is that product code runs on any Python 3.8+ machine, with pywinpty the LONE platform exception, lazily imported in pty_manager only. journal.py importing msvcrt at module level creates a second platform-bound module and a distro-scan exception nobody approved. Specify the same idiom as the existing exception: lazy platform-guarded import with an fcntl.flock (or O_APPEND-atomicity) fallback on POSIX — the fix is one line in the plan now versus a distro-gate surprise in Phase 3.

findings.topic: accelerated 20-greens guts the flake gate's premise
findings.message: The 20-consecutive-greens rule exists to catch time- and environment-dependent flakes before a walk joins the unattended 5AM run — quiescence races, overnight state, cold-start conditions. Explicitly allowing 20 accelerated back-to-back runs in one warm session 'to count' removes exactly the variance the gate samples for: a walk that flakes only against a cold service, a concurrent Foreman build, or the 5AM scheduled-task environment passes 20-in-a-row trivially. Steel-manned, the accelerated mode is fine as a FAST-FAIL filter but should not fully substitute: require some minimum of genuinely separated runs (e.g. ≥5 across distinct service restarts or nights) within the 20 before the walk is promoted.

findings.topic: interpolation-census scope vs the >20 threshold is ambiguous
findings.message: The census classifies 'EVERY {…} interpolation in generate_html and render_project_window_html' — but those functions generate the ENTIRE page, including the server-rendered HTML body (task rows, project tiles, lane columns), which is interpolation-dense by design and NOT in C1's extraction scope (C1 names the JS/CSS blobs + the window shell). Read over the whole renderers, '>20 markup-emitting interpolations' is a near-certain trip — the amendment gate fires as a foregone conclusion, not a contingency. Read over only the extraction-scoped blobs, the threshold is plausible. The plan must pin the threshold's denominator to the extraction-scoped regions explicitly, or Phase 0 mechanically manufactures a spurious proposal-to-John amendment before Phase 1 ever starts.

findings.topic: warn-mode soak coverage on a single-user service
findings.message: A 'soak day' of warn-mode on a service with exactly one human user samples only the routes John happens to touch that day plus the healthcheck's walk. Rarely-used mutating routes (grass_export, move_project, term_delete, the .bat/.vbs launcher paths, scheduled tasks) may produce ZERO warn-log lines, and the gate then reads absence-of-warnings as safe-to-enforce — a false negative by construction. The Phase-0 consumer-enumeration inventory is the real evidence; the plan should say the enforce flip is gated on the INVENTORY having a verified token path per consumer, with the warn log demoted to a tripwire for consumers the inventory missed, not promoted as the primary gate artifact.

findings.topic: path-audit misses git's own worktree metadata
findings.message: The path-audit tool scans DURABLE STORES (registry folder_path, worktree_path, discovery.json, job dirs) for absolute paths — but if the managed worktree base lives under ANCHOR_DATA_DIR and relocates, git itself holds absolute paths in a store the audit doesn't name: each main repo's .git/worktrees/<name>/gitdir and each worktree's .git file both point absolutely at each other. A rewrite of the registry's worktree_path without `git worktree repair` (or equivalent) leaves every parked/idle worktree — the ones W6 deliberately preserves across restarts — git-broken after the move, failing exactly the warm-resume path the boot-reaper dry-run is protecting. Add git worktree metadata to the audit's scan list and `git worktree repair` to the migration script, or state explicitly that the worktree base does not live under ANCHOR_DATA_DIR and therefore does not move.

Phase 0 bills the contract shim as its ONE behavior-bearing deploy, but the same phase also deploys the drain script into the live smoke ritual, injects sentinel comments via a pre-wave commit, and wires the ANCHOR_BUILD script tag into BOTH renderers (a change to the two most fragile functions in the codebase, pre-census, pre-freeze). The claim is rhetorically tidy but the renderers edit in particular deserves the same parity care Phase 1 formalizes — say that, rather than classifying it as non-behavior by fiat.
